title: Auditing Citation Grounding in LLM-Generated OCT Reports Using Public Data: Evaluation Framework Study (Preprint)
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND

Evidence tags and structured schemas are often used to make large language model (LLM)-generated clinical text appear grounded. However, the presence of an evidence tag does not by itself establish that the tagged sentence is supported by the cited evidence. Health AI evaluation therefore needs methods that separate formatting compliance from semantic consistency and clinical truth.

 OBJECTIVE

This study aimed to evaluate a public-data audit framework for citation-grounded optical coherence tomography (OCT) report generation and to test whether schema input adds measurable audit value beyond explicit citation instructions.

 METHODS

Using the first 50 parseable public MORG report excerpts, we derived English evidence schemas and ran a four-arm computational ablation: free text without citation, free text with citation, schema without citation, and schema with citation. A local Gemma 4 model generated reports. A deterministic scrutinizer measured evidence-tag presence, invalid tags, lexical alignment, and evidence-field coverage. Three local LLM judges screened sentence-level semantic consistency, and a distractor test probed scope control. Results were analyzed descriptively.

 RESULTS

Citation-enabled arms achieved complete tag presence, whereas no-citation arms produced no tagged sentences. Schema plus citation improved lexical alignment compared with free text plus citation (0.857 vs 0.617) and improved mean evidence-field coverage (0.996 vs 0.952). The free-text citation arm missed 8 of 157 derived evidence fields, compared with 1 of 157 in the schema-citation arm. Across 226 tagged sentences, exact pairwise judge agreement ranged from 0.942 to 0.978 and Gwet AC1 ranged from 0.941 to 0.977. Distractor uptake was 0/50.

 CONCLUSIONS

Citation instructions drove tag behavior, while schema input improved auditability and completeness checks. The framework should be interpreted as a language-layer health AI evaluation method, not as image-interpretation validation, clinical grounding, or deployment safety evidence.

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) can turn a flood of cross-layer industrial logs into a fluent incident narrative, but a narrative that cites only real, resolvable events can still be wrong in every relation that matters: the login came from a different workstation, the write command occurred after the physical change it supposedly caused, the action fell inside a planned maintenance window, and the controller does not even actuate the affected process. A cited event is not necessarily supporting evidence. When such a narrative drives automated response, the error propagates into isolating the wrong controller or revoking a legitimate operator. We present EviGuard, a system that decides when an LLM’s understanding is trustworthy enough to act on. EviGuard stores auditable cross-layer evidence in a provenance graph, lets the LLM propose only hypotheses, compiles each hypothesis into atomic machine-checkable claims in an Incident Claim Language, and has an ensemble of deterministic verifiers label every claim supported, contradicted, or unknown against the graph—honoring interval time, event-time policy and credential versions, network reachability, and physical control dependencies. A response gate forbids any high-impact action whose critical preconditions are not all supported. On EviCPS-Bench (42 hardware-in-the-loop attack chains, 9600 claim-level labels, κ=0.87), EviGuard cuts the unsupported-claim rate from 12.6% to 1.7%, raises relation-edge F1 from 0.64 to 0.89, holds prompt-injection success to 0.4%, and executes zero unverified high-impact actions across 3200 response decisions, at a median end-to-end latency of 0.44 s.</jats:p>

title: Embedding qualitative data in LLM semantic space: A tutorial on conceptualization, measurement, and validation
items.abstract: Large language model embeddings give any text coordinates in a semantic space, where the cosine between two coordinates indexes their similarity. Standard qualitative practice cannot quantify such closeness: open-ended answers become nominal variables, which represent only difference under dummy codes. Psychometrics obtains such closeness from responses, as the correlations among a scale's items. Whether the cosine can substitute for the correlation is therefore open. We tested it against established findings in open data, each with an agreed structure: the Big Five, PANAS in two languages, Schwartz's values, Pineo-Porter occupational prestige, and the ISEAR and Kjell narratives. Linguistic structure alone did not reproduce the psychometric structure. The item texts recovered part of it, and none of it where a relation carries a sign. They fall far short of a random split-sample ceiling. Read from the other side, that is a finding about questionnaires: a scale's wording does not carry what its respondents give it. Embeddings supply a semantic layer between raw language and conventional coding, where the material that neither psychometrics nor hand coding reaches belongs. A category label—an occupation, a diagnosis, a brand—becomes coordinates rather than a dummy variable. An open-ended answer becomes coordinates without a coder. Cut into segments, a long answer becomes a path, along which departures, returns, and drifts can be drawn and tested. What any of it means, however, stays with the analyst. We supply the conceptual background, an R package, and a tutorial: no training, no Python.

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to revolutionize various domains, including personalized wellness sales, by integrating structured enterprise knowledge into their frameworks. In this context, we introduce Data2Dialogue, a framework designed specifically for enhancing LLMs' conversational abilities through structured data integration. By leveraging diverse sources of enterprise knowledge, Data2Dialogue enables LLMs to provide tailored product recommendations that cater to individual wellness needs. The approach incorporates advanced knowledge extraction and contextualization techniques to ensure the information delivered is both relevant and responsive to users' inquiries in real-time. A multi-step inferencing process enhances the LLM's grasp of enterprise-specific knowledge while improving dialogic engagement. Experimental results indicate that Data2Dialogue leads to higher customer satisfaction and increased sales conversions compared to conventional methods. By grounding LLMs in structured knowledge, the framework fosters more accurate and context-rich interactions, effectively aligning user inquiries with product offerings.</jats:p>

title: Measuring Self-Rating Bias in LLM-Generated Survey Data: A Semantic Similarity Framework for Independent Scale Mapping
items.abstract: <jats:p>Synthetic survey data generated by large language models (LLMs) offers a promising com plement to traditional survey research, but existing approaches suffer from a fundamental circularity: the same model family that generates text responses also maps them to numeri cal scales. We introduce Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR), a framework that decouples text generation from scale mapping by using embedding-based cosine similarity against predefined anchor statements. A pilot configuration study (N = 17, 3 domains) revealed that naturalis tic behavioral anchors outperform formal survey jargon by 29 percentage points, asymmetric embedding adds a further +6 pp, and anchor quality is the single most impactful design factor. Cross-validation on an expanded 69-case test set across 8 domains yields 65% exact match and 91% within ±1. A direct LLM baseline (Claude Haiku 4.5, temperature = 0) achieves 87% exact match on the same benchmark, establishing that SSR’s contribution is methodological independence rather than accuracy superiority. A pre-registered circularity experiment (N = 345 generated texts, 5 personas × 69 cases) demonstrates that this in dependence matters empirically: LLM self-rating produces 4-fold compressed error variance (σ2 = 0.21 vs. 0.87 for SSR) and systematic directional bias, confirming that self-rating cir cularity is not merely a theoretical concern. We release the full calibration dataset, anchor library (15 semantic families), and framework as open-source tools.</jats:p>

title: Symmetry-Aware Knowledge Graph Compression for LLM Grounding via Symbolic Retrieval
items.abstract: <jats:p>We exploit graph automorphism orbit partitions for lossless knowledge graph (KG) compression and graph-native retrieval within a single self-describing binary artifact. The Symmetry-Aware Compression (sac) pipeline identifies vertex orbits via the Nauty individualization-refinement algorithm, encodes non-representative nodes as within-orbit residuals, and routes five semantically homogeneous streams through independent DEFLATE stages. The resulting sacf format achieves up to 34.1× lossless compression on standard KG benchmarks and outperforms the graph-native HDT format by +52% on a heterogeneous banking KG with ∼3,000 non-trivial orbits. HDT in turn outperforms sacf on KGs dominated by singleton orbits, where its bit-packed adjacency already captures the available redundancy. This split is empirical and informative: sacf's contribution is specifically in the regime where many entities share local schemas but carry distinct attribute payloads, the profile typical of banking, legal, and medical enterprise knowledge graphs. Crucially, unlike gzip or xz which produce opaque blobs, the same artifact decodes directly into a queryable in-memory graph, eliminating the need for a separate database, vector index, or ingestion pipeline. A relevance-scored BFS interface extracts predicate-typed subgraph context and injects it into LLM prompts for symbolically grounded LLM inference. Ablation studies confirm that retrieved context is the primary performance driver: withholding it collapses link-prediction Hits@1 to zero across three standard benchmarks; with context, the system achieves 0.566 on WN18RR using Llama-3.1-8B, matching the same-backbone trained baseline SSQR (0.559) zero-shot. On a financial reasoning benchmark (80 questions, 14 categories), sacf-based retrieval matches text-chunk RAG overall (69/80 each) while dominating policyconstraint detection (3/4 vs. 0/4), demonstrating the advantage of explicit structural grounding for relational reasoning tasks where exact predicate-level evidence is required.</jats:p>

title: Privacy-Preserving Natural Language Analytics over Sensitive Tabular Data Using Semantic Grounding and Multi-Stage Privacy Validation
items.abstract: <jats:p>Natural-language interfaces allow users to query structured datasets without requiring knowledge of database query languages. Existing approaches, however, concentrate on query generation and execution and offer limited protection against semantic ambiguity, unsafe requests, and privacy violations. This paper presents a privacy-preserving framework for natural-language analytics over structured data that combines LLM-based intent extraction with deterministic analytical execution. Semantic grounding and schema validation resolve the request; a two-layer privacy guardrail then validates the request before execution and assesses the returned result for disclosure risk. Because the model produces only a structured analytical plan, no model-generated SQL or executable code reaches the data. The implementation centralizes model settings and disclosure thresholds in configuration and derives schema metadata from the loaded dataset. Evaluation on a 100-query healthcare benchmark produced 95.00% semantic-grounding accuracy and 100.00% final-decision accuracy, with a mean end-to-end runtime of 3.1152 seconds. The framework provides policybased disclosure-risk reduction rather than a formal privacy guarantee.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>This article examines how TEI-based digital archives and human-curated annotation layers can support documented uses of large language models in literary analytics. It argues that structured textual infrastructures strengthen the conditions for evaluating and interpreting LLM outputs by making scholarly decisions explicit, inspectable, auditable, and contestable. Here, semantic data governance refers to provenance, documentation, controlled vocabularies, interpretive criteria, and critical evaluation. The case study is the LdoD Archive and its Virtual Edition “Philosophical Intertextuality,” built on TEI-encoded sources for Fernando Pessoa’s Livro do Desassossego, a fragmentary and posthumously assembled work. The virtual edition adds a human-authored semantic layer through taxonomies and tagging tools that connect fragments with philosophical categories and named thinkers. Building on this architecture, the article proposes a layered workflow in which TEI, taxonomies, authority records, annotation tables, machine-readable metadata, and validation procedures interact. A curated dataset derived from the virtual edition can support qualitative comparison between human annotations and model outputs, exploratory evaluation of omissions, unsupported associations, and interpretive divergences, and prompt design based on concise scholarly examples. The annotations function as situated scholarly claims, allowing interpretive plurality to coexist with stronger provenance, inspection, and critical assessment in transparent and reproducible conditions for future LLM-assisted literary analysis across different analytical contexts.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming cognitive interfaces to data lakes, enterprise knowledge bases, vector memories, browsers, files, and software tools. This shift creates a data-governance gap: an agent may reason over large private context, yet the protected resource often lacks a verifiable record of which user intent, data object, action, destination, and semantic release were authorized. This paper proposes CapAgent, a semantic data-flow governance middleware for LLM agents in big-data cognitive-computing environments. CapAgent maps human-attested task intent into signed, attenuable, and purpose-bound capability tokens that are checked by a reference monitor before sensitive tool invocation, memory retrieval, data export, and inter-agent delegation. Its policy layer combines task templates, resource labels, destination rules, caveats, semantic release modes, and audit obligations; its runtime enforces both symbolic scope checks and semantic recoverability checks over protected facts. We present formal governance semantics, a conservative intent compiler, an explainable data-flow decision workflow, and a runnable Python middleware. A reproducible trace-replay benchmark with 600 benign and adversarial traces across five data-intensive agent scenarios reports attack success, benign success, false blocking, latency, component ablations, and audit quality. In this synthetic trace-replay evaluation, the full monitor reduces measured attack success from 100.00% under ambient execution and 12.50% under scope-only authorization to 0.00% (Wilson 95% CI [0.00, 0.95]), while retaining 75.00% benign success. In addition, we conduct a 520-trial end-to-end tool-calling benchmark with representative prompt-only, task-shield-style, CaMeL-style, scope-only, and full-CapAgent configurations; a 210-task compiler gold-standard evaluation; a 240-item semantic-release calibration set; and a 12-cell BDCC-style scalability microbenchmark. In these supplemental tests, full CapAgent obtains 0.00% ASR (95% CI [0.00, 1.06]) in the tool-calling benchmark, 87.50% exact-policy compiler match with 0.00% over-authorization, 88.89% semantic-release recall with 0.00% false-block rate, and sub-millisecond in-process authorization latency up to 100,000 resources. The results support CapAgent as an auditable governance layer for cognitive LLM agents rather than as a replacement for model-level alignment or public end-to-end agent benchmarks.</jats:p>

title: Verifying LLM-Generated Data-Pipeline Transformations: A Hybrid Static–Semantic Approach for Leakage and Data-Quality Faults
container-title: International Journal For Multidisciplinary Research
items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate data-pipeline and feature engineering transformations from natural-language specifications. This introduces a new and under-examined risk surface: transformations that are syntactically valid and schema-correct yet semantically wrong, silently injecting temporal leakage, granularity errors, join fan-out, silent row loss, and data-quality defects. Existing text-to-SQL verifiers target the correctness of a single natural-language-to-SQL query and do not address transformation- and pipeline-level data-flow faults, which today are caught only reactively—after a model trained on a leaking feature posts implausible offline accuracy. We make three contributions. First, we define a six-category fault taxonomy for generated transformations grounded in real feature-engineering failure modes. Second, we propose a lightweight hybrid verifier that combines static dataflow analysis with semantic execution checks, including a gold-free metamorphic leakage test: removing future rows must not change any historical feature value. Third, we build a fault-injection benchmark on synthetic and real (Rossmann Store Sales) data and evaluate against a static validation baseline and a strong LLM-as-judge baseline. The hybrid verifier attains perfect precision (no false alarms), is deterministic and inexpensive, and detects structural, temporal, and granularity faults; a strong LLM-as-judge attains higher overall recall on semantically subtle faults but over-flags correct transformations and is blind to granularity errors. The two approaches are complementary, motivating combined verification for trustworthy LLM-generated data pipelines.</jats:p>

items.abstract: Modern cloud-native systems generate heterogeneous observability data at unprecedented scale, yet two critical gaps persist in operational intelligence. First, distributed analytical consumers independently reconstruct metric definitions from physical storage schemas, producing inconsistent results across dashboards, pipelines, and LLM-based incident analysis systems. Second, automated root cause analysis frameworks lack a governed, semantically coherent data foundation, causing diagnostic drift when agents query the same metric through divergent pipelines. This paper presents the Integrated Observability Intelligence Framework (IOIF), a unified architecture that couples a Python-native semantic layer with a hierarchical multiagent Large Language Model (LLM) orchestration system. The semantic layer enforces metric consistency through breadth-first search (BFS) join resolution, time-to-live (TTL)-governed caching with portable logical cache keys, and row-level security (RLS) enforcement at the model boundary. Three integration mechanisms bridge the layers: Semantic Context Injection (SCI), Portable Cache Key Propagation (PCKP), and Security Context Threading (SCT). Experimental evaluation on production-scale observability workloads across 350 systematically injected failure scenarios demonstrates a 23.4% reduction in false positive diagnoses and a 31.2% improvement in investigation consistency relative to frameworks operating on ungoverned raw metrics, with a mean time-to-diagnosis of 7.8 minutes.

title: FEW-AI-SERIAL: A Domain-Agnostic Semantic Compression Protocol for LLM Prompt Injection and IoT Data Encoding
items.abstract: <jats:p>We present FEW-AI-SERIAL, a domain-agnostic semantic compression protocol that reduces structured data payloads by 68-92% while maintaining full human readability and native interpretability by Large Language Models (LLMs). Unlike binary serialization formats (Protocol Buffers, Avro, CBOR) that achieve comparable compression but produce opaque byte streams, FEW-AI-SERIAL uses positional mnemonic keys (2-3 uppercase characters) and domain-native value notation to produce compact text that both humans and LLMs can read without external schema or decoder. We validate the protocol across three production domains: (1) LLM few-shot prompt injection for poker decision-making (86% token reduction, 100% extraction accuracy), (2) IoT sensor data encoding on ESP32 microcontrollers (92% byte reduction, 10 bytes per reading vs. 120 bytes JSON), and (3) Model Context Protocol (MCP) agent-to-agent communication (88% message size reduction). Empirical benchmarks using Claude Haiku demonstrate that LLMs interpret FEW-AI-SERIAL with identical accuracy to JSON (100% vs. 100%) while consuming 41% fewer bytes and responding 31% faster. To our knowledge, no existing protocol simultaneously achieves sub-Protobuf compression ratios, native LLM interpretability, and human readability without requiring schema compilation or code generation.</jats:p>

title: Behavioral Retrieval-Augmented Tutoring
From Evidence to Action: A Systematic Study of External Knowledge Grounding in LLM-based Agents
items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language model (LLM)-based agents consult documents and databases, maintain memory, call tools, and alter external state. Access alone does not establish that the consulted information governs behavior: an agent may retrieve the applicable policy and ignore it, cite a source that does not support an action, or store its own inference as fact. We study this problem as external knowledge grounding: the use of externally checkable knowledge to support and constrain reasoning, planning, and action. A structured scoping review of seven frozen topical and bibliographic resources and a seed matrix yielded 2,169 records. After deduplication, 1,833 records were screened; 101 reports were assessed in full and 100 sources were included. We separate 71 core LLM-agent studies, 20 transferable antecedents, and nine contextual surveys or specifications, and use only the core stream for coverage counts. The analytical framework follows six functions-Acqire, Align, Integrate, Act, Verify, and Update-across factual, entity, procedural, policy, environmental, and experiential knowledge. In the core corpus, 64 studies cover acquisition and all 71 integration, but only 18 implement a runtime check and 31 address persistent update. Contribution-role sensitivity preserves the gap: all 18 runtime checks occur among 56 non-evaluation-primary reports, while none of 15 benchmark/evaluation-primary reports exposes one. title: Semantic Grounding Index: Geometric Bounds on Context Engagement in RAG Systems
items.abstract: <jats:p>When retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems hallucinate, what geometric trace does this leave in embedding space? We introduce the Semantic Grounding Index (SGI), defined as the ratio of angular distances from the response to the question versus the context on the unit hypersphere \({\mathbb{S}}^{d - 1}\). Our central finding is _semantic laziness_: hallucinated responses remain angularly proximate to questions rather than departing toward retrieved contexts. On HaluEval (\(n = {5,000}\)), we observe large effect sizes (Cohen’s \(d\) ranging from \(0.92\) to \(1.28\)) across five embedding models with mean cross-model correlation \(r = 0.85\). Crucially, we derive from the spherical triangle inequality that SGI’s discriminative power should increase with question-context angular separation \(\theta{(q,c)}\)—a theoretical prediction confirmed empirically: effect size rises monotonically from \(d = 0.61\) (low \(\theta{(q,c)}\)) to \(d = 1.27\) (high \(\theta{(q,c)}\)), with AUC improving from \(0.72\) to \(0.83\). Subgroup analysis reveals that SGI excels on long responses (\(d = 2.05\)) and short questions (\(d = 1.22\)), while remaining robust across context lengths. Calibration analysis yields ECE \(= 0.10\), indicating SGI scores can serve as probability estimates, not merely rankings. A critical negative result on TruthfulQA (AUC \(= 0.478\)) establishes that angular geometry measures topical engagement rather than factual accuracy. SGI provides computationally efficient, theoretically grounded infrastructure for identifying responses that warrant verification in production RAG deployments.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>In knowledge graph construction tasks, recent research often leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of unstructured data processing. However, current LLMs rely on lexical co-occurrence statistical patterns, making it difficult to capture deep semantic relationships. Furthermore, existing research largely focuses on entity-relation extraction or semantic-level optimization, overlooking the inherent hierarchical logical structures within text paragraphs (e.g., chapter organization, paragraph coherence). This leads to insufficient semantic completeness and damaged structural consistency in the constructed knowledge graphs. To address this dual limitation, we propose LLM-S2KG, a semantic–structural information extraction method that integrates LLMs with semantic correlation analysis. This method achieves synergistic modeling of semantic depth and logical structure by simultaneously performing dual parsing of keywords and structure, discovering and completing semantic associations, and finally integrating these dual graphs for construction. Experiments show that in query tasks, LLM-S2KG improved the F1 score by 0.1183, 0.1412, and 0.0231 compared with KeyBERT, TF-IDF, and LLM-KG, respectively. In fill-in-the-blank QA tasks, it achieved an accuracy of 94.81%; and in open-ended QA tasks, an accuracy of 85.885%, moderately outperforming LLM Triple Extraction (73.308%), LLM Triple Extraction with Source Sentence Augmentation (80.085%), and Chroma Database Import (76.150%). In summary, LLM-S2KG provides a unified modeling paradigm for structured knowledge extraction using LLMs, featuring mutual empowerment and co-evolution of semantics and structure.</jats:p>

title: Semantic Network Sharing in Human Versus LLM Discussion Groups
items.abstract: Using a corpus of 51 mock-jury discussion groups, we analyzed the discussion process of human groups and then compared it with that of large language model (LLM) groups in an exploratory analysis. The task was a hidden profile task, solvable only by combining information distributed across members. We examined solution-path attainment and the sharedness of the word-level semantic network (the cross-member edge ratio: the proportion of edges linking words introduced by different members) in relation to the information-sharing process. Human discussion progressed from individual to group-level sharing: an information-sharing phase in which intra-individual semantic networks remained (cross-member edge ratio .34), followed by an information-integration phase in which network links became shared across members (.54), and a decision phase (.66). In LLM groups calibrated to human behavioral statistics, this three-phase structure was radically compressed, lacking the human allocation of time. Under a memory constraint, however, the individual-to-group sharing shift observed in humans emerged. A stepwise prompt ladder reproduced the reported collapse of LLM collective reasoning and identified the constraints that avert it. Moreover, the association between the sharedness of the semantic network and solution-path attainment found in human groups (ρ = +.52, n = 50) was not observed in LLM groups (n = 8 per condition). These differences are interpreted as showing the contrast between human groups, which come to share a semantic network gradually through discussion, and LLM groups, which share a knowledge structure from the outset.

title: ACREF: LLM-as-a-Judge Guided Data Curation and Semantic Evaluation for Automated Code Refinement
items.abstract: <jats:p>Context: Automated code refinement modifies source code in response to natural-language review comments. Existing approaches commonly rely on review--revision pairs mined from repository histories, treating developer revisions as supervision targets and evaluation references. However, such revisions are observational records rather than manually verified solutions and may be incomplete, misaligned with review intent, or functionally inconsistent.Objectives: This study investigates the reliability of repository-derived review--revision pairs and aims to improve the quality of supervision and semantic evaluation for automated code refinement.Methods: We propose \ModelName{}, an LLM-guided data curation framework that integrates static filtering, semantic filtering, refinement-specific quality assessment, generative reconstruction, and post-reconstruction verification. The curated supervision is further used to train two task-specific models: CR-Metric, a semantics-aware evaluator, and CR-Refiner, a code refinement model.Results:  On CodeReviewer, ACREF increases the average internal rubric-based score from 3.21 to 4.50 on a five-point scale, corresponding to a relative increase of 40.25\%. As the same rubric guides both curation and assessment, this result is treated as an internal optimization signal. A score-blinded human audit of 500 reconstructed samples finds that 77.0\% are rated as clearly improved. CR-Metric achieves 78\% exact agreement, 99\% within-one-point agreement, and an average correlation of approximately 0.67 with human ratings, substantially outperforming conventional lexical-overlap metrics in alignment with human judgments. CR-Refiner achieves competitive reference-based performance on CodeReviewer and CodeReviewer-New and consistently outperforms its static-filtered counterpart.Conclusion: Pair-level curation improves the usefulness of repository-derived supervision for automated code refinement and provides a basis for more semantics-aware evaluation. The findings also indicate that LLM-guided curation should be complemented by independent human or execution-based validation when stronger functional-correctness claims are required.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Industrial data-center systems contain complex component dependencies and long fault-propagation chains, making accurate root-cause localization difficult. Large language models (LLMs) provide a promising solution because of their strong ability to understand, organize, and reason over heterogeneous operational evidence. However, existing LLM-based methods mainly rely on statistical co-occurrence in pretraining corpora and may mistake correlation for causation in complex systems. In this paper, we propose CALM, a causally constrained LLM framework for fault diagnosis. The main idea is to learn the causal structure among fault units induced by system dependencies and use it to constrain the LLM reasoning process. Specifically, we train a graph neural network with independently learnable edge gates, impose sparsity directly on these gates, and validate the retained edges using post-training nonlinear Granger predictive gains. The resulting causal relationships constrain the LLM to trace root causes reliably. Experiments on a dataset collected from a power metering data center show that the proposed method achieves a root-cause localization accuracy of 82.6%, outperforming the best-performing baseline by 9.2 percentage points. The method also outputs explicit fault-propagation paths, indicating that causal-structure constraints can improve both the accuracy and interpretability of fault diagnosis.</jats:p>

title: VeriQuant: Measuring Numerical Reliability of LLM Agents in Quantitative Derivatives Pricing via Verified Tool-Grounding and Ambiguity Benchmarking
items.abstract: <jats:p>We introduce VeriQuant, an oracle-grounded benchmark and evaluation framework for measuring and characterising LLM reliability on quantitative finance tasks. Using an independently deterministic Black-Scholes pricing engine as ground truth, we evaluate Claude Sonnet 4.6 across four complementary tiers: numeric precision (Tier 1, n=40), conceptual reasoning (Tier 2, n=30), ambiguity recognition (Tier 3, n=23), and a second-pass auditor agent (Tier 4, 63 audit calls over existing Tier 1 and Tier 3 responses). Without tool access, the model achieves 75% accuracy on numeric computations and 100% / 96.7% direction and reasoning accuracy on conceptual questions, but exhibits a systematic 0% failure rate on vega—consistently omitting the ÷100 unit-conversion step required by market convention despite explaining this convention correctly in the conceptual tier. Tool-grounding raises numeric accuracy to 100% (+25 pp), confirming that execution errors—not conceptual gaps—drive failure. On the ambiguity tier, tool access improves handling scores from 39.1% to 50.0% (+10.9 pp), primarily by enabling explicit clarification requests. A key negative finding emerges: making the dividend-yield parameter q "required" in the tool schema failed to trigger the intended AMBIGUOUS_INPUT error because the model infers reasonable defaults rather than omitting the field—demonstrating that JSON schema enforcement is insufficient to surface ambiguity with current LLMs. Finally, we test whether a second, tool-free LLM call reviewing the solver's own response can catch these errors: the auditor catches only 1 of 10 unit-convention self-contradictions and 5 of 18 silently-assumed ambiguities, and—independently verified against a from-scratch reimplementation of Black-Scholes—its own proposed corrections are themselves wrong in both cases where it incorrectly flagged a correct solver answer. Taken together, VeriQuant separates four distinct failure classes (arithmetic, unit-convention, ambiguity specification, and unreliable self-review), provides a reusable taxonomy and benchmark, and yields actionable design lessons for practitioners deploying LLM agents in quantitative financial workflows.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Industrial maintenance systems generate large volumes of fault records that are typically stored as unstructured textual descriptions, making automated analysis and solution recommendation challenging. This study presents an AI‐assisted framework with two complementary components for Turkish industrial maintenance data: semantic clustering of fault descriptions and LoRA‐based generation of corrective‐action suggestions. Fault descriptions are transformed into semantic representations using multiple embedding methods, reduced with Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP), and clustered with HDBSCAN. Under the fixed UMAP‐HDBSCAN configuration reported in this study, Language‐Agnostic Sentence Representations (LASER) obtained the strongest internal clustering results, including a Silhouette score of 0.8529. For recommendation generation, Meta‐LLaMA‐3‐8B, Phi‐4, Gemma‐3n‐E4B, and T5‐base were fine‐tuned with Low‐Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and evaluated using ROUGE metrics. Among the evaluated models, Phi‐4 achieved the highest lexical‐overlap scores (ROUGE‐1 = 0.3320, ROUGE‐2 = 0.1915, ROUGE‐L = 0.3128, and ROUGE‐Lsum = 0.3127), followed by Meta‐LLaMA‐3‐8B. In the reported generation experiment, cluster identifiers, LASER distances, and retrieved historical actions were not supplied as additional Large Language Model (LLM) input; consequently, the present results should not be interpreted as evidence that clustering causally improves generation quality. Moreover, ROUGE measures lexical similarity rather than technical correctness, executability, or safety. The framework is therefore positioned as a decision‐support approach whose generated recommendations require domain‐expert verification before operational use.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Temporal Knowledge Graph Inference (TKGI) is a cornerstone for intelligent decision-making in dynamic scenarios, but existing models face critical bottlenecks, including inadequate complex-context modeling, a lack of entity importance quantification, insufficient novel-event reasoning accuracy, and weak domain adaptability. To address these issues, this study proposes a semantics-enhanced model (LLM-DSaR) integrating Large Language Models (LLMs), temporal attention networks, and optimized contrastive learning. Specifically, a two-stage LLM semantic enhancement (LLM1 + LLM2) framework first generates structured semantic analysis reports via adaptive prompt engineering, and then extracts domain-specific semantic embeddings from the last-layer hidden states through pooling and linear projection, which are further fused with TransE-based structural embeddings; meanwhile, LLM2 mitigates data sparsity in novel-event reasoning; a dynamic weight fusion (DWF) framework adaptively assigns feature weights to achieve deep feature synergy; an LLM-enhanced contrastive-learning module strengthens event clustering and discrimination. items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced semantic computing by enabling systems to interpret and generate natural language with high flexibility. However, they remain limited in solving real-world problems that require precise computation, reliable data access, and structured optimization. Tasks such as route planning, geospatial reasoning, and combinatorial optimization highlight these shortcomings, particularly in terms of factual grounding and solution feasibility. This paper proposes a framework for tool-augmented semantic computing, in which LLMs are combined with external data sources and specialized algorithmic components. The framework consists of a semantic layer for interpreting user intent, a tool layer for data access and computation, and an orchestration layer coordinating their interaction. By using travel planning as a representative use case, we demonstrate how tasks such as point-of-interest selection, coordinate retrieval, and route optimization can be decomposed into modular processing steps. In particular, route sequencing is formulated as a variant of the traveling salesman problem, requiring dedicated optimization beyond the capabilities of LLMs. The results show that integrating semantic reasoning with data grounding and algorithmic optimization enables reliable solutions to complex real-world problems, highlighting the potential of hybrid AI systems for future semantic computing applications.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The paper discusses semantic data replication in geo-distributed systems, in which only semantically relevant fragments of data are propagated between regions, rather than all state changes. Unlike classical approaches (key-based replication, partitioning, rulebased selective replication), the authors propose using semantic representations—vector embeddings, LLM-based relevance scoring, and semantic tagging—to drive replication decisions at the level of event or change streams (log/CDC). The article introduces semantic eventual consistency: replicas tend toward a state that is sufficient relative to a region’s semantic profile rather than full identical copies everywhere. Key trade-offs among latency, cross-region transfer cost, and semantic completeness are examined, together with architectural patterns (semantic routing; hybrid digest with on-demand fetch) and risks such as non-determinism, model drift, filtering errors, and security or data-localization concerns. The contribution is conceptual and frames terminology and avenues for further research into semantic replication mechanisms.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper investigates whether structured collaboration between multiple large language models (LLMs), each assigned a distinct cognitive role grounded in psychological theory, produces benefits beyond simple answer aggregation. We propose the Parallel Synthesis architecture, in which three cognitively specialized roles Analyzer (hierarchical decomposition), Creative (divergent thinking), and Critic (critical evaluation) process each task independently and in parallel, and a Synthesizer integrates their outputs into a final response. To evaluate collaborative reasoning, we introduce the Emergent Reasoning Score (ERS), a composite metric that separates perspective integration (Synthesis Effectiveness) from novel concept generation (Emergent Value). Experiments on the AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC-Challenge) (1172 questions) and and the Massive Multitask Language Understanding benchmark (MMLU) (1531 questions) show two consistent findings. First, the architecture achieves high Synthesis Effectiveness (SE=0.711–0.744), indicating reliable integration of all three cognitive perspectives. Second, Emergent Value remains low (EV=0.096–0.112), indicating that synthesis primarily recombines existing concepts rather than generating substantial novel content. A Majority Voting baseline achieves comparable or slightly higher answer accuracy than the Synthesizer on both benchmarks, showing that the architecture’s main contribution lies not in answer selection but in producing integrated reasoning traces that draw on multiple perspectives. These findings suggest that the practical value of cognitively grounded multi-agent architectures lies in reliable perspective integration, while ERS provides a reusable framework for distinguishing integration from genuinely novel reasoning in multi-agent LLM systems. The empirical results reported here constitute a pilot validation of the proposed framework on closed-form benchmarks, intended to establish a proof of concept and motivate larger-scale evaluation.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Industrial control systems (ICSs) face escalating security challenges due to evolving cyber threats and the inherent limitations of traditional intrusion detection methods, which fail to adequately model spatiotemporal dependencies or interpret complex protocol semantics. To address these gaps, this paper proposes DLG–IDS—a lightweight intrusion detection framework that innovatively integrates dynamic graph construction for capturing real–time device interactions and logical control relationships from traffic, LLM–driven semantic enhancement to extract fine–grained embeddings from graphs, and a spatio–temporal graph neural network (STGNN) optimized via sparse attention and local window Transformers to minimize computational overhead. Evaluations on SWaT and SBFF datasets demonstrate the framework’s superiority, achieving a state–of–the–art accuracy of 0.986 while reducing latency by 53.2% compared to baseline models. Ablation studies further validate the critical contributions of semantic fusion, sparse topology modeling, and localized temporal attention. The proposed solution establishes a robust, real–time detection mechanism tailored for resource–constrained industrial environments, effectively balancing high accuracy with operational efficiency.</jats:p>

title: A Study on LLM-driven Knowledge Graph Construction and Production Anomaly Inference for Semantic Standardization of Multi-factory Data in Automotive Manufacturing
items.abstract: <jats:p>Multi-plant automotive-component data contain inconsistent field names, device codes, quality codes, and unstructured production logs. This study presents an LLM-driven method for manufacturing semantic standardization and knowledge-graph reasoning. Equipment signals, production beats, quality inspections, maintenance work orders, VIN/OCR results, shutdown events, and process files are integrated to construct crossfactory semantic mapping tasks. Sentence-BERT and GPT-4o-mini perform field alignment and context correction; BERT-CRF supports entity extraction, while GraphSAGE and R-GCN infer typed anomaly relations. KG-RAG and an LLM Agent are further used for quality tracing and case retrieval. Experiments cover 4 plants, 9 production lines, 156 field categories, 780,000 production records, and 120,000 maintenance and quality texts. Under leave-one-factory-out evaluation, Sentence-BERT plus GPT-4o-mini achieves 94.1% field-matching accuracy and 94.6% precision. The 94.1% accuracy is 21.3 percentage points above rule-based mapping at 72.8%, corresponding to a 29.3% relative improvement. GraphSAGE-R-GCN obtains Hits@10 of 0.876 on the mixed split and 0.842 under factory holdout. The complete KG-RAG-Agent system reaches retrieval P@20 of 0.842, R@20 of 0.816, and 92.1% answer accuracy, while reducing mean anomaly-tracing time from 2.8 h to 54 min. These results show that semantic constraints and typed graph reasoning support cross-factory anomaly transfer and evidencegrounded knowledge reuse.</jats:p>

title: Instruction-Augmented Referring Expression Grounding and LLM-Based Planning for Human–Robot Collaboration
items.abstract: <jats:p>Human-robot collaboration (HRC) is central to flexible and intelligent manufacturing, particularly under the trend of mass personalization. However, existing language-driven approaches typically rely on predefined commands or assume that human instructions align precisely with the physical scene, which limits robustness when instructions are vague, incomplete, or inconsistent with the environment. To address this limitation, we propose an instruction-augmented framework that couples vision-language perception with large language model (LLM)-based planning. The framework comprises three components: an MLLM-based question generation network (MLQGN) that detects instruction ambiguity and proactively raises a clarifying question; a cross-modal perception network that grounds the clarified instruction to a pixel-level mask of the target object through adapter-based tuning; and an LLM planner enhanced by retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that produces executable action sequences via structured robot APIs and retrieved domain knowledge. Extensive experiments in an epicyclic gear train (EGT) assembly scenario, together with evaluations on the public benchmarks, demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach. Results show significant improvements in correction accuracy and planning robustness. The proposed method provides a reliable and flexible solution for intelligent HRC systems in advanced manufacturing.</jats:p>

title: Governance State as a First-class Signal: A Social Media Knowledge Governance Grounding Framework for the LLM Consumption Chain
items.abstract: <jats:p>As large language models become the primary consumption interface for social content, the governance outcomes accumulated by platforms (adjudications, debunking records, community annotations) do not enter the generation chain, giving rise to three types of paraphrasing hallucinations. To address this problem, a consumption-side governance grounding framework (CGG) is proposed. CGG treats governance state as a first-class signal, instantiating three types of evidence-adjudication, feedback, and evolutionfrom public governance records, fusing them into a content-indexed governance state registry, reducing queries to a four-valued state {support, refute, pending, absent}, and executing direct, conditional, disclosing, and annotating responses via a response policy ladder, with execution strictness regulated by domain risk weights. Experiments on the CHEF and CED datasets show that governance signals drive policy-ladder-consistent behavior: the governance-driven arm achieves 90%~100% on refute/pending/absent states, while governance-free arms achieve only 0%~4.5%; the governance arm attains 100% grounding rate in citing adjudication reasons versus 45.5% for the retrieval-only baseline; and in decoupling experiments, the external signal stably drives attribution-type behaviors such as disclosure and annotation (above 90% conformity across configurations, reaching 100% when a refute signal is injected into truthful content), yet it cannot force the model to endorse truth values against strong content priors (conformity drops to 52% when a support signal is injected into rumor content). The framework offers a consumption-side governance route for mitigating LLM hallucinations in social scenarios, where trust flows with content and is presented at use time rather than recomputed at inference time.</jats:p>

However, LLMs often struggle to determine which retrieved documents are relevant and how they relate to one another. We argue that this difficulty arises from a semantic gap between retrievers and LLMs due to differences in their training objectives and architectures. Notably, ConRAG is suitable for low-resource scenarios where LLMs and retrievers are frozen. Further analysis shows that retriever-derived information helps the LLM better identify relevant evidence and model relationships among documents, leading to more effective generation. items.abstract: <jats:p>Multi-source heterogeneous data in discrete manufacturing shop floors, including vibration signals, equipment logs, visual monitoring data, and handwritten production reports, exhibit significant differences in modality and semantic representation. Traditional fusion methods often fail to bridge the semantic gap between low-level sensing signals and high-level manufacturing cognition, limiting intelligent anomaly analysis and decision-making capability. To address this issue, this paper proposes a semantic translation and fusion framework for industrial heterogeneous data based on Knowledge Graph (KG), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and Large Language Models (LLMs). First, a unified semantic translation mechanism is developed to convert multimodal industrial data into structured semantic representations for cross-modal alignment. Second, an industrial knowledge graph and RAG mechanism are introduced to integrate process knowledge, maintenance manuals, and historical fault records into the reasoning process. Third, an LLM-driven reasoning framework is designed for multimodal semantic fusion, anomaly identification, causal analysis, and optimization recommendation generation. In addition, a digital twin-based visualization interface is constructed to realize real-time interaction between production lines, industrial data, and intelligent cognitive reports. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly improves industrial reasoning accuracy, anomaly analysis correctness, and response efficiency compared with general-purpose LLMs, providing an effective solution for intelligent cognition and decision-making in discrete manufacturing systems.</jats:p>

affiliation.name: University of Nottingham Nottingham

items.abstract: <jats:p>Existing geospatial data formats such as GeoJSON, Well-Known Text (WKT), and CityGML, are optimised for geometric computation and rendering. While effective for Geographic Information Systems (GIS), these approaches present limitations when used with Large Language Models (LLMs). For example, coordinate arrays carry no inherent semantic meaning, spatial relationships require computational geometry to extract, and the human experience of place is usually absent. This manuscript introduces foundational work on Geospatial Experience-Oriented Notation (GEON), a text-based format that bridges machineoptimised geospatial data and human-readable spatial descriptors. GEON encodes identity, geometry, purpose, experiential qualities, spatial relationships, temporal patterns, and data provenance in a readable and structured syntax designed for human comprehension and LLM reasoning. This manuscript presents the initial specification, reference implementations in Python, Rust, and JavaScript, and an empirical evaluation demonstrating how GEON achieves 20% fewer tokens than equivalent GeoJSON files, while encoding 31% more semantic facts per token. This manuscript explores the implementation and how LLMs reason about place-making, urban design interventions, and spatial intelligence tasks that existing formats struggle to support.</jats:p>

title: SemanticAIMapper: Deterministic-First Semantic Mapping through Structured LLM Planning and Validation
items.abstract: <jats:p>Semantic mapping is required whenever multiple structured representations of the same domain must be aligned across storage, interfaces, messaging, analytics, or application layers. Many correspondences can be resolved deterministically, but renamed, abbreviated, nested, or project-specific fields remain difficult to align reliably at scale. Large language models (LLMs) offer useful semantic inference for these residual cases, yet unconstrained generation is difficult to audit and can violate structural, semantic, and policy constraints. This paper presents SemanticAIMapper, a deterministic-first mechanism in which an LLM is used only as a bounded planner for unresolved semantic correspondences. The mechanism first resolves exact and high-certainty relations locally, then constructs a schema-grounded request for the remaining targets. This request combines an invariant planning instruction with a structured task specification containing source and target schemas, unresolved targets, candidate correspondences when available, and optional example-value context for disambiguation. The model is required to return a structured alignment plan under a fixed response schema rather than free-form text. A downstream acceptance boundary interprets the returned content, normalizes it into a candidate plan, and validates it against schema consistency, uniqueness constraints, admissible transformation vocabulary, and confidence policy before any AI-proposed alignment is accepted. The contribution is therefore not a language-specific realization, but a portable interaction pattern for trustworthy LLM-assisted semantic mapping. The paper formalizes the request and response patterns, explains how bounded semantic planning is maintained, and discusses how project-specific adaptation may improve planning quality without changing the deterministic core.</jats:p>

                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Semantic Table Annotation,</jats:italic>

While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at these tasks, their scalable deployment is hindered by prohibitive costs, high latency, and privacy information leakage. Distilling LLM capabilities into compact local models offers a viable solution; however, these models inevitably overfit to the structured noise in the teacher's predictions. In this paper, we formalize the setting of label-efficient distillation from noisy LLMs. Our empirical analysis reveals two error patterns: (1)

To address these, we propose e SemDistill, a framework that bootstraps high-performance local annotators from noisy LLM outputs using only scarce trusted anchors. e SemDistill uses reliability-based partitioning and tier-specific optimization: it models global drift with anchor-guided correction, profiles residual hallucinations through learning trajectories, and trains trusted, semi-trusted, and noisy tiers with different objectives. Extensive experiments demonstrate that e SemDistill effectively addresses the cost-quality trade-off. It outperforms the LLM teacher (GPT-5-mini) and the distillation baseline while reducing inference costs by

                  <jats:p>Adoption of automated quality control in the textile and apparel industry has lagged owing to inherent features, such as labor-intensive tasks and deformability of flexible fabrics. Precise detection and localized diagnosis of sewing stitch defects remain critical challenges because existing datasets often provide only image-level labels or focus exclusively on raw fabric anomalies. Therefore, we propose StitchingNet-Seg, a comprehensive, large-scale semantic segmentation dataset designed for industrial sewing processes. Derived from the StitchingNet dataset, this dataset comprises 10,836 images covering 11 representative fabric types, 7 defect classes and 1 normal class (8 classes in total). Each image is annotated with pixel-level masks to capture intricate geometric features. To validate the usability and technical quality of the dataset, benchmark experiments are conducted using representative convolutional neural network-based architectures and vision transformer-based models. The evaluation results demonstrated robust overall learnability across diverse architectures. However, they also revealed relatively lower segmentation performance on specific defect classes characterized by subtle thread tension variations and 3D structural deformations. This confirms that StitchingNet-Seg provides a reliable foundation for developing intelligent automated optical inspection systems for the global garment industry.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The quest to answer complex questions, those requiring both structured facts and contextual evidence from unstructured data, has shown a gap in knowledge systems: the incompatibility between symbolic and semantic inference. Knowledge Graphs (KGs) support formal, logically grounded querying via structured languages such as SPARQL. Conversely, LLMs (Large Language Models) and semantic text search offer broad knowledge coverage through vector-based similarity metrics. However, beyond using KGs for refining text or LLM results, and complementing missing information in KGs via LLMs or text search, there is less emphasis on accessing LLMs & semantic text search functionality through SPARQL. Moreover, existing Question Answering (QA) methods on heterogeneous data sources use RAG, data unification, and decompose-and-aggregate methods. The unifying approaches suffer from irreversible information loss; decomposition-driven methods are prone to cascading errors; and RAG methods lack explainability and are limited to shallow textual integration. Therefore, we introduce KGXL-Query, a new SPARQL functionality extension that embeds LLMs and semantic search directly into SPARQL, enabling hybrid inference where symbolic and non-symbolic methods coexist within a single, executable, and explainable framework. Additionally, KGXL-Query paves the way by transforming the question to leverage the model rather than altering the data to fit it. Our experiments on four heterogeneous QA datasets show that KGXL consistently outperforms existing methods across all four benchmarks.</jats:p>

title: UrbanAct-GPT: LLM-Based Activity and Role Semantic Inference from Mobile Phone Signalling Data for City-Scale Weekday Dynamic Urban Structure Analysis
items.abstract: <jats:p>Mobile phone signalling and other passive-sensing mobility data offer broad coverage at low cost, yet they typically contain only location information and lack activity semantics. In contrast, travel surveys provide fine-grained labels (e.g., trip purposes) but are costly and unsuitable for continuous city-scale diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we propose UrbanAct-GPT, which leverages large language model (LLM) to infer period-level activity types and day-level population roles using only readily available POIs and mobile signalling data. UrbanAct-GPT integrates data engineering, Context-constrained Chain-of-Thought (C-CoT) prompt engineering, and QLoRA parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) to enrich location-only trajectories with interpretable semantic information. Validation on an independent test set (n = 150) shows high and stable performance, achieving 0.95 activity accuracy (Weighted avg F1 = 0.96) and 0.70 role accuracy (Macro avg F1 = 0.71). Comparative experiments quantify the contribution of each component: relative to a baseline prompt, C-CoT improves Activity accuracy from 71.7% to 81.6% and Role accuracy from 42.0% to 52.7%; QLoRA yields further gains to 89.8% (Activity) and 63.3% (Role). Applying UrbanAct-GPT to a typical weekday in Shanghai (approximately 2.1 million users) reveals a diurnal activity-based urban structure: daytime Work activity concentrates in the inner city and key corridors (e.g., Caohejing–Hongqiao; Lujiazui–Jinqiao–Zhangjiang), while night-time activity shifts to residential belts around the central-city boundary; parts of Pudong show notable day–night Work–Home overlap. Overall, UrbanAct-GPT provides a scalable pathway for dynamic urban-structure identification and population-oriented refined planning and governance.</jats:p>
